questions.question_stem: A client on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has a routine INR of 4.8. No bleeding is noted. What does the nurse do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Hold the warfarin and notify the provider

options.label: B
options.text: Give vitamin K immediately

options.label: C
options.text: Give the warfarin — the level is therapeutic

options.label: D
options.text: Encourage vitamin K-rich foods to balance the level

questions.rationale_correct: 4.8 is above the usual 2.0–3.0 therapeutic range, but a high INR with NO bleeding is not an emergency reversal case.

rationale_incorrect.B: vitamin K is a provider-ordered decision, and reversing a non-bleeding client fully re-exposes them to clot risk.
rationale_incorrect.C: 4.8 is not therapeutic — giving the dose pushes it higher.
rationale_incorrect.D: dietary vitamin K works against warfarin, slowly and unpredictably — it is never the fix for a supratherapeutic INR.

questions.question_stem: A client has a chest tube connected to a closed drainage system. The nurse notes continuous bubbling in the WATER-SEAL chamber. What does this most likely mean?

options.label: A
options.text: This is normal and expected

options.label: B
options.text: There is an air leak in the system or the client's lung

options.label: C
options.text: The suction is set too high

options.label: D
options.text: The tube is ready to be removed

questions.rationale_correct: bubbling belongs in the SUCTION-CONTROL chamber (gentle, continuous). The water-seal chamber should only bubble intermittently, with exhalation/cough.

rationale_incorrect.C: suction level shows in the suction chamber, not the water seal.
rationale_incorrect.D: an air leak is a reason to assess and report — not remove.

questions.question_stem: A client with SIADH has a sodium of 118 mEq/L and new confusion. Which action is the priority?

options.label: A
options.text: Encourage oral fluids to flush the excess sodium

options.label: B
options.text: Institute fluid restriction and seizure precautions

options.label: C
options.text: Start a rapid IV bolus of hypotonic fluid

options.label: D
options.text: Recheck the sodium in one week

questions.rationale_correct: in SIADH the problem is water retention diluting the sodium — the client is not short on fluid, they are drowning in it.

rationale_incorrect.A: more fluid dilutes the sodium further.
rationale_incorrect.C: hypotonic fluid makes hyponatremia worse, and rapid shifts in sodium are dangerous in either direction.
rationale_incorrect.D: Na 118 with confusion is symptomatic — it is acted on today.

questions.question_stem: A client with preeclampsia is receiving magnesium sulfate. Respirations are 10/min, deep tendon reflexes are absent, and urine output is falling. What does the nurse do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the infusion — it is not working yet

options.label: B
options.text: Stop the infusion and prepare calcium gluconate

options.label: C
options.text: Document the findings and reassess in one hour

options.label: D
options.text: Give a fluid bolus to increase urine output

questions.rationale_correct: RR 10 + absent reflexes + falling output is the magnesium toxicity triad. The drug level is too high — the infusion is the problem.

rationale_incorrect.A: increasing the infusion deepens respiratory depression.
rationale_incorrect.C: these are toxicity signs, not chart-and-wait findings.
rationale_incorrect.D: fluids do not reverse magnesium toxicity; calcium gluconate is the antidote, and the infusion stops first.

questions.question_stem: The day after a total thyroidectomy, a client reports tingling around the mouth and in the fingertips. The nurse elicits a positive Chvostek sign. Which problem is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypercalcemia from overactive parathyroids

options.label: B
options.text: Hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury or removal

options.label: C
options.text: Hypokalemia from poor oral intake

options.label: D
options.text: Hypermagnesemia from antacid use

questions.rationale_correct: the parathyroids sit on the thyroid — surgery that removes the thyroid can take calcium regulation with it. Tingling + Chvostek = low calcium.

rationale_incorrect.A: hypercalcemia does not cause perioral tingling or Chvostek.
rationale_incorrect.C: hypokalemia causes weakness and cardiac changes, not this picture.
rationale_incorrect.D: hypermagnesemia causes depressed reflexes and sedation — nearly the opposite presentation.

questions.question_stem: Which post-operative client does the nurse see FIRST?

options.label: A
options.text: Day 1 after hip replacement, reporting pain 6/10 at the incision

options.label: B
options.text: Day 2 after abdominal surgery, now suddenly short of breath with sharp chest pain

options.label: C
options.text: Day 1 after appendectomy, asking for more ice chips

options.label: D
options.text: Day 3 after hernia repair, ready for discharge teaching

questions.rationale_correct: sudden dyspnea + sharp chest pain on post-op day 2 is the classic pulmonary embolism picture — immobility plus surgery is the setup.

rationale_incorrect.A: expected post-op pain is real, but it is not an airway/breathing threat.
rationale_incorrect.D: discharge teaching is important and completely schedulable.
